user.title: What would you like to add?
user.description: Preset modes hold the modes, presets hold the values, and preset blueprints hold parameter definitions that presets share. Each kind lives in its own hub, and the hub appears with the first object you add to it.

preset_mode.title: New preset mode
preset_mode.description: A preset mode holds a set of modes that belong together, for example Home, Away and Night. Its presets are added afterwards, and every further preset mode becomes an entry of its own.

data_description.name: For example "House Mode" or "Window State".
data_description.modes: Type a name and press enter to add your own modes.

blueprint.title: New preset blueprint
blueprint.description: A blueprint defines parameters once - a target temperature, a boost duration - and hands them to every preset that follows it. Those presets follow every later change of the blueprint and have no parameters of their own; their values per mode stay their own.

manage_parameters.title: Parameters of the preset blueprint
manage_parameters.description:
One row per parameter. Use the pencil to rename a parameter, to change its type or to give it an icon, the bin to delete it. The order of the rows is the order of the entities.

Every preset following this set is updated right away. Deleting a parameter also deletes its stored values in those presets, and changing its type does the same, because the old values no longer fit.

data_description.device_class: Tells Home Assistant what the number means, which enables unit conversion and long-term statistics. Only units matching the device class are allowed.

data_description.default: Used when a mode has no value for this parameter.

preset.title: New preset
preset.description: A preset holds one set of values per mode, for one device or one scenario. It follows a preset mode, which decides which of its values are valid right now.

data_description.preset_mode: Which dimension decides the active mode. Can be left empty and assigned later.
data_description.blueprint: With a blueprint the preset takes over its parameters and stays tied to it: they are then edited on the blueprint, for every preset following it at once.

data_description.preset_mode: A preset without a preset mode keeps its parameters, its values and its modes - only nothing decides which mode is active, so its values do not resolve. Switching to another preset mode keeps the values stored under the modes both have in common.

assign_blueprint.title: Assign preset blueprint
assign_blueprint.description:
With a blueprint the preset takes over its parameters and follows every change of it. Pick “-” to leave the blueprint: the preset keeps the parameters it has right now as its own and can edit them again.

Switching blueprints replaces the parameters of the preset. Values are kept wherever a parameter of the same key exists in the new blueprint.

duplicate.description: The copy gets the parameters of "{name}" and the values stored for them, mode by mode. It follows the same preset mode and, if there is one, the same blueprint.

user.title: New preset mode
user.description: A preset mode holds a set of modes that belong together, for example Home, Away and Night. Its presets are added afterwards, and every further preset mode becomes an entry of its own.

data_description.name: For example "House Mode" or "Window State".
data_description.modes: Type a name and press enter to add your own modes.

manage_modes.title: Modes
manage_modes.description:
The list is worked through from top to bottom: the first mode whose conditions match becomes active. Drag a row by its handle to change the priority, use the pencil to rename it or set its conditions, and the bin to delete it.

A mode without conditions always matches, so it catches everything below it - put one at the bottom to have a fallback mode. If nothing matches at all, no mode is active and every preset reports “unknown”.

data_description.source_entity: Leave empty to let the preset mode decide for itself. With an entity, its state names the active mode - matched against the mode names, case insensitive - and nothing else is evaluated: the conditions are ignored, there is no automatic switch and no selector. A state that names no mode leaves the preset mode without an active mode. So this needs an entity whose state is literally one of your mode names - a dropdown helper with the modes as its options is the typical case. A sensor reporting a number or a measurement will never match one.

duplicate.title: Duplicate preset mode
duplicate.description: The copy gets the modes and the conditions of "{name}". It does not get the entity that one follows: two preset modes reading the same entity would always hold the same mode.

assign_presets.title: Presets of “{name}”
assign_presets.description: Every preset listed here follows this preset mode. Adding one moves it here if it followed another; the preset mode it currently follows is in brackets. Taking one off leaves it with its parameters, its values and its modes, but without an active mode - it then asks for a new preset mode in the repairs.

orphaned_preset.title: Preset "{preset}" has no preset mode
orphaned_preset.description:
Nothing decides which mode is active for this preset, so its values do not resolve. Either it was created without a preset mode, or the one it followed was deleted - in which case it kept its parameters, its values and its modes.

Assign it a preset mode: Settings > Devices & services > Preset Manager > Presets, then the preset, then “Assign preset mode”.

manual_mode_deleted.title: Preset "{preset}" lost the mode it was set to
manual_mode_deleted.description:
It was set by hand to "{mode}", and that mode has been deleted from its preset mode. A preset that holds nothing is not held at all - it would follow every switch of its preset mode with a switch that says it does not - so its automatic is back on and it follows its preset mode again.

If it should stand on its own, switch the automatic of the preset off and pick one of the remaining modes.
